events.title: The martyrdom of Sts. Peter and Paul at Rome
events.shortBlurb: Tradition holds that the two great Apostles gave their lives at Rome under Nero, consecrating the city with their blood…
body: By the constant tradition of the Church, the Apostles Peter and Paul were put to death at Rome during the persecution of Nero, in or about the year 67. Peter, the first bishop of Rome, was crucified — according to ancient testimony at his own request head downward, thinking himself unworthy to die as his Master had — on the Vatican hill; Paul, as a Roman citizen, was beheaded on the road to Ostia.

Over their tombs rose the great basilicas of St. Peter and of St. Paul Outside the Walls, and their martyrdom in the capital of the empire came to be seen as the founding witness of the Roman Church. Their common feast has been kept at Rome since at least the third century.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles”

events.title: Pius IX convokes the First Vatican Council
events.shortBlurb: By the bull Aeterni Patris the pope summoned the first general council of the Church in three centuries…
body: On 29 June 1868, the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul, Pope Pius IX issued the bull Aeterni Patris convoking the First Vatican Council, the first ecumenical council since Trent had closed three hundred years before. The bishops of the world were summoned to Rome to meet the errors of the age and to set forth the doctrine of the Church.

The Council opened on 8 December 1869 and in 1870 solemnly defined the primacy and the infallible teaching authority of the Roman Pontiff. It was suspended when Italian troops occupied Rome that September, and was never formally reconvened.
